titre: Half the nitrogen in your body comes out of a factory
accroche: A reaction developed in 1909 now feeds nearly half of humanity, and was used to kill
contenu_vulgarise:
The air you breathe is 78% nitrogen. Your proteins and your DNA are full of it. And yet, for almost the entire history of life, that nitrogen was out of reach.

The reason lies in a bond. In air, nitrogen travels in pairs of atoms welded together by a triple bond, one of the strongest in chemistry. Neither a plant nor an animal can break it. Only a few bacteria manage to, slowly, and this bottleneck capped harvests for millennia.

## Forcing an equilibrium that doesn't want to go

Combining the nitrogen of air with hydrogen to make ammonia is possible on paper. In practice, the reaction yields traces.

Fritz Haber attacks the problem with the three levers available to a chemist. He heats, so that the molecules have the energy to break the triple bond. He compresses, to several hundred times atmospheric pressure, because the reaction turns four molecules into two, and high pressure pushes an equilibrium toward the side that takes up the least room. He adds a catalyst, iron-based, which opens a cheaper path without being consumed.

The first lever works against the other two: heat, necessary for speed, works against the equilibrium. The process lives in that compromise, around 400 to 500 degrees.

In 1909, Haber obtains a continuous trickle of ammonia on a laboratory bench. The same year, Carl Bosch takes up the problem for BASF: making that pressure hold not on a bench but at the scale of a factory. It will take him about four years; the first industrial plant starts up at Oppau on September 9, 1913. The two will receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, in 1918 and 1931.

## What it changed

Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer lifted the ceiling. It now supplies a major share of the protein consumed in the world, and it is estimated that nearly half of the nitrogen in a human body has passed through this process.

The wording deserves a pause. This is not an economic dependence: the atoms themselves, in your muscles, were torn from the air by an industrial reaction. No other technology is so literally inscribed in our tissues.

## The downside

The same process supplies nitrates, and nitrates make explosives. Germany in 1914, cut off from Chilean saltpeter by the blockade, held out thanks to synthetic ammonia, in a war that shortage would have cut short. Haber himself personally directed the use of chlorine as a weapon at the front in 1915.

And the environmental ledger is not settled. Some of the nitrogen spread on fields runs off into rivers, where it feeds algae whose decomposition consumes oxygen and leaves dead zones. The synthesis also consumes a notable fraction of the world's natural gas.

Here is a rare case: a reaction of which one can say both that it made billions of people's existence possible, and that it durably damages the environment in which they live. Neither of these two sentences cancels the other.

repere.texte: Haber files his patent on the “synthesis of ammonia from its elements” on October 13, 1908. A century later, 40 to 50% of the protein consumed in the world relies on the nitrogen he made available.
repere.source: Erisman, Sutton, Galloway et al., “How a century of ammonia synthesis changed the world,” Nature Geoscience, 1, 2008

carte.punch: It is estimated that nearly half of the nitrogen in your body has passed through a factory.
carte.idee: The nitrogen in air is locked by a triple bond that no plant can break. The Haber-Bosch process, born in 1909, breaks it at 400 to 500 °C under several hundred times atmospheric pressure, and now supplies 40 to 50% of the protein consumed in the world.

quiz.question: Why does the process work under very high pressure?
choix: Because pressure keeps the ammonia formed from breaking back down as it leaves
Because the iron catalyst becomes active only above a certain pressure threshold
Because the reaction turns four molecules into two, and pressure pushes toward that side
Because air must be compressed to extract the nitrogen before reacting it
quiz.explication: Compressing a gas equilibrium shifts it toward the side that takes up the least volume: here, two molecules of ammonia against four of reactants. High pressure partly offsets the heat, which is necessary for speed but unfavorable to yield. The catalyst, for its part, speeds things up without shifting the equilibrium, and separating nitrogen from air is a distinct step.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who turned Haber's reaction into an industrial process, and for which company?
choix: Fritz Haber himself, for the University of Karlsruhe
Carl Bosch, for the German company BASF
Wilhelm Ostwald, for a Franco-German consortium
Justus von Liebig, for the Prussian state
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that Carl Bosch takes up the problem in 1909 for BASF, and starts the first industrial plant at Oppau on September 9, 1913.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What role did Fritz Haber personally play during World War I, beyond his chemical discovery?
choix: He negotiated the 1918 armistice on behalf of Germany
He refused any military involvement and went into exile in Switzerland
He personally directed the use of chlorine as a weapon at the front in 1915
He ran the production of Chilean saltpeter imported by ship
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that Haber personally directed the use of chlorine as a weapon at the front in 1915, a downside of the same process that feeds humanity.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What proportion of the nitrogen in a human body has, according to the entry, passed through the Haber-Bosch process?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry puts forward that nearly half of the nitrogen in a human body has passed through this industrial process, a figure literally inscribed in our tissues.
